source: Kapoor et al. (2025) Prediction of Item Difficulty for Reading Comprehension Items by Creation of Annotated Item Repository
finding: A penalized regression on annotated linguistic, test and context features recovers item difficulty well. LLM embeddings add little on top.
numbers: 1,076 NY/TX grade 3-8 reading items, 2018-23. Test RMSE 0.59 vs baseline 0.92. Pearson r 0.77. ModernBERT embeddings alone r 0.76, RMSE 0.62; all features r 0.77, RMSE 0.61. Earlier content-based work reached r 0.3-0.7.
quote: Prediction of item difficulty based on its text content is of substantial interest.
limits: Target is state-level p-value, rescaled to an IRT-like scale. Reading only. Linguistic features and embeddings overlap, so one set is enough.
agent_relevance: A cheap S0 difficulty estimate from text is feasible, but one cheap feature family already captures most of the signal. Do not stack estimators.

source: Yaneva et al. (2024) BEA shared task on USMLE item difficulty, as reported in Kapoor et al. (2025)
finding: BEA 2024 shared task on medical exam items shows how little text-only prediction beat a dummy baseline.
numbers: 667 USMLE items: best RMSE 0.29 vs dummy 0.31. A 12,038-item USMLE study: best RMSE 22.45 vs 23.65 baseline.
limits: Second-hand, taken from the Kapoor et al. text. Not read at source.
agent_relevance: Expect text-only difficulty prediction to be weak in knowledge-heavy domains. Treat S0 as a triage signal.

source: Razavi & Powers (2025) Estimating Item Difficulty Using Large Language Models and Tree-Based Machine Learning Algorithms
finding: Asking GPT-4o for one difficulty rating works only moderately. Having the LLM extract cognitive and linguistic features, then fitting trees, works better.
numbers: N=5,170 K-5 math and reading items (Rasch scale). Direct GPT-4o, all grades pooled: math r .83, RMSE 0.91 (dummy 1.01); reading r .81, RMSE 0.86 (dummy 1.04). Feature-based RF/GBM math: r .87, RMSE 0.83 / 0.81. GBM cut RMSE 18.5% vs the dummy across grades.
limits: Pooled r is inflated by grade differences. Within grade, direct-LLM fit was poor for early grades: math grade 1 R2 0.003, reading grade 1 R2 0.019. Math grade K error was worse than a grade-mean dummy.
agent_relevance: Pooled correlations across levels flatter the estimator. Judge an S0 estimator within a difficulty band, against a grade-mean style baseline.

source: Razavi & Powers (2025) Estimating Item Difficulty Using Large Language Models and Tree-Based Machine Learning Algorithms (baselines and model choice)
finding: Structured LLM features beat text-statistic baselines. Grade metadata alone is already a strong baseline.
numbers: Math RMSE: metadata-only RF 1.12, TF-IDF+RF 1.01, dummy 1.01, direct LLM 0.91, full RF 0.83. Four LLMs screened on 250 items (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, Llama 3.2, Claude-3-haiku); GPT-4o chosen on RMSE and r. Temperature 0. Feature-model math r by grade .37 to .70.
limits: Pilot model screen was small (n=250) and not tabulated.
agent_relevance: Mirror this pattern in S0: the LLM fills named feature slots, and code does the regression or lookup. This fits our rule that the model fills slots and code decides.

source: Scarlatos et al. (2025) SMART: Simulated Students Aligned with Item Response Theory for Question Difficulty Prediction
finding: Simulated students, aligned to IRT ability by DPO, predict open-ended item difficulty better than direct LLM prediction.
numbers: Smarter Balanced (open-ended reading): SMART on Llama-3.2-1B PCC .649, SCC .486, RMSE .670; kNN on SBERT PCC .596; ICL kNN Llama-3.1-70B PCC .527; ICL random 70B PCC .12. CodeWorkout: SMART 1B PCC .308; ICL random 70B PCC .249.
limits: CodeWorkout correlations stay low (about .3 to .4). Small base models. Needs real response data for alignment training.
agent_relevance: Difficulty emerges from simulated attempts, not from a judged label. Same idea as running cheap rollouts to size a problem, with the check coming from a scoring model.

source: Scarlatos et al. (2025) SMART: Simulated Students Aligned with Item Response Theory for Question Difficulty Prediction (zero-shot vs tuned simulation)
finding: Zero-shot simulated students are poor; alignment is what makes simulation useful.
numbers: Smarter Balanced, 1B: response generation zero-shot PCC .265, SFT .562, SMART .649. 3B zero-shot PCC .345, SMART .674.
limits: Same limits as above.
agent_relevance: Unaligned role-play is a weak difficulty meter. Prefer measured outcomes (pass rates) over persona prompts.

source: Acquaye et al. (2026) Take Out Your Calculators: Estimating the Real Difficulty of Question Items with LLM Student Simulations
finding: LLMs are poor direct judges of difficulty, but simulated classrooms fitted with IRT track real NAEP difficulty.
numbers: 631 NAEP math MCQs, grades 4/8/12. Best simulation r up to .75 / .76 / .82 (ensemble). Direct prompting correlations between -0.139 and 0.137 for every model, GPT-4o also weak. Text-embedding baselines rho 0.36 (grade 4), 0.30 (grade 12), -0.04 (grade 8). Gemma-2-9b r .69 at grade 4; Llama-3-8b r .42-.44.
limits: Open models plus a GPT-4o check. NAEP correct rates are population averages. Class size and prompt matter.
agent_relevance: Direct difficulty judgment by the model has near-zero signal on math MCQs; simulate and aggregate instead.

source: Acquaye et al. (2026) Take Out Your Calculators: Estimating the Real Difficulty of Question Items with LLM Student Simulations (design factors)
finding: Diverse named students beat student ids. Bigger classes and ensembling raise correlation. Bigger models are not always better.
numbers: Named diverse students Pearson .60-.72 vs ids .57-.67 range and no identifier .57-.67 as reported across grades. Gemma-2-9b grade 4: r .62 at class 50 to .69 at class 300. Ensemble rho .70-.74; weighted ensemble rho .82 at grade 12. Gemma 9B equals 27B at grade 4 (r .69 both). Content area: Measurement rho .75-.88, Algebra .45-.64 at grade 8.
limits: Gains from names are modest and may reflect prompt diversity, not demographics.
agent_relevance: Diversity of attempts and averaging help; one persona does not. This echoes our rule that samples from one model are not independent.

source: Zhu et al. (2025) The LLM Already Knows: Estimating LLM-Perceived Question Difficulty via Hidden Representations
finding: Difficulty as the target model sees it can be read from its own first hidden state with one forward pass, no sampling.
numbers: Markov-chain value function over hidden states. Reported ScienceQA ROC-AUC 93.09 and macro-F1 79.48 with Qwen2.5-VL-7B; beats self-rating prompt, answer-consistency (AG), LLMs-ranking and HaluSearch baselines on most of 8 datasets, at lower test-time cost.
limits: Results table was scrambled in text extraction, so only the quoted headline figures are certain. Ground truth is 3 rollouts matching the answer. Needs white-box access.
agent_relevance: Closest match to S0: a cheap pre-solve difficulty read that could drive how much search to spend. Needs hidden states, so not usable with a closed API agent.

source: Zhu et al. (2025) The LLM Already Knows: Estimating LLM-Perceived Question Difficulty via Hidden Representations (transfer limit)
finding: A probe trained in one domain loses accuracy in another, and each target LLM needs its own probe.
numbers: The paper reports a notable drop in ROC-AUC and macro-F1 in its cross-domain test.
limits: Exact values not recovered from the scrambled table.
agent_relevance: Calibrate any S0 estimator per task family before trusting it.

source: Brant, Kuhn & Pang (2026) Estimating Exam Item Difficulty with LLMs: A Benchmark on Brazil's ENEM Corpus
finding: Ten LLMs rank ENEM items by IRT difficulty only weakly and underestimate difficulty.
numbers: 1,031 ENEM items vs official IRT. Best Spearman per model: Claude-4-Sonnet .33, GPT-4o .31, o3 .37, Gemini-2.5-Flash .35, Gemini-2.0-Flash .31. Mean predictor RMSE 1.19 with rho 0; model RMSE 1.70-2.25. Per-subject best rho about .29-.37.
limits: Items translated, images transcribed to text. Prompt choice effect is as large as model choice.
agent_relevance: Low RMSE can hide zero rank power. Judge S0 by rank correlation, and expect about rho .3 from judged difficulty.

source: Brant, Kuhn & Pang (2026) Estimating Exam Item Difficulty with LLMs: A Benchmark on Brazil's ENEM Corpus (prompt, modality, calibration)
finding: Prompt wording shifts results as much as switching model. Image items hurt, and a constant shift fixes bias but not ranking.
numbers: 76 model-prompt pairs: RMSE rises 1.26 (SD 0.95) on image items; 56 of 76 pairs significant; Hedges g -0.17; mean rho change -0.05. Raw predictions shifted downward (too easy). A fitted constant on 5-fold CV reduces RMSE; ranks unchanged. Country cues amplified underestimation.
limits: The modality penalty may be loss in the image-to-text pipeline.
agent_relevance: Recalibrate the level, but expect the ranking to be the limiting part.

source: Ding et al. (2025) Easy2Hard-Bench: Standardized Difficulty Labels for Profiling LLM Performance and Generalization
finding: Six datasets with continuous difficulty from human IRT or Glicko-2 and from LLM leaderboard IRT. LLM accuracy falls as difficulty rises.
numbers: Human-based: E2H-AMC (IRT), Codeforces and Lichess (Glicko-2). LLM-based IRT: GSM8K, ARC, Winogrande. Six LLMs evaluated; accuracy decreases with difficulty on all sets; model gaps widen at high difficulty on GSM8K; Claude-3-Opus beat GPT-4-Turbo on hard Lichess puzzles, reversing the trend.
limits: E2H-ARC here is the science-QA ARC, not the abstraction corpus. Its difficulty is LLM-side. Model differences are small on ARC and Winogrande.
agent_relevance: Gives a graded difficulty axis we can use to check S0 against ground truth.

source: Ding et al. (2025) Easy2Hard-Bench: Standardized Difficulty Labels for Profiling LLM Performance and Generalization (GPT-4 as difficulty judge)
finding: GPT-4 pairwise difficulty judgments agree with humans on large-gap pairs but rank poorly against IRT.
numbers: Matching accuracy GPT-4 vs human: GSM8K .922, ARC .825, Winogrande .771. IRT vs human: .942 / .737 / .734. Spearman IRT vs GPT-4: GSM8K .612, ARC .218, Winogrande .164.
limits: Pairs were filtered to large gaps, so matching accuracy overstates ranking skill.
agent_relevance: An LLM judge is fine for coarse easy-versus-hard splits and bad for fine ordering. Use only as a coarse S0 gate.

source: Jain et al. (2025) Exploring the Potential of Large Language Models for Estimating the Reading Comprehension Question Difficulty
finding: GPT-4o and o1 answer reading items almost perfectly, and their difficulty ratings are compressed toward the middle versus IRT.
numbers: SARA dataset: human students 87.57% mean accuracy, GPT-4o 98.84%, o1 99.14%. IRT difficulty spread wide; GPT-4o narrower; o1 most compressed.
limits: Ceiling effect. Short workshop paper; I found no correlation coefficient in the text read.
agent_relevance: If the solver is near ceiling, its own performance carries no difficulty information. Difficulty has to be defined for the solver in use.

source: Hoyl (2026) Synthetic Student Responses: LLM-Extracted Features for IRT Difficulty Parameter Estimation
finding: Predict simulated student responses with a neural net, then derive IRT difficulty. LLM-extracted pedagogical features add the most.
numbers: 250,000+ maths responses. Holdout Pearson 0.7791, Spearman 0.7606. Ablation Pearson: embeddings only .6822; plus question features .6842; plus option features .6758; plus LLM features .7791.
limits: Single maths dataset.
agent_relevance: LLM-extracted features such as solution step count and misconceptions carry the gain. Basic text features add nothing once embeddings are in.

source: An & Wang (2026) Student Use of LLMs and the Limits of AI-Generated Question Difficulty in Data Science Courses
finding: LLM-assigned Easy/Medium/Hard labels on its own generated questions do not predict real difficulty.
numbers: 378 questions authored (126 per label), 311 deployed, 7,888 responses from 54 students. Difficulty label vs Bloom level Spearman 0.90. Label vs empirical difficulty rho 0.06; Bloom vs empirical 0.02.
quote: The ratings reflect the structural formatting of a question rather than its underlying difficulty.
limits: One course. High overall accuracy limits score variance. Labels co-generated with Bloom tags.
agent_relevance: Self-assigned difficulty labels reflect formatting, not difficulty. Never let the model label its own problem easy or hard without outcome data.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) EIP: Weighted Ranking of LLMs by Quantifying Question Difficulty
finding: Difficulty derived from which models fail a question, propagated both ways between models and questions, matches human difficulty judgments better than IRT.
numbers: 30 models, 35,550 questions. 90% agreement with human judgments (better than a simple-rank baseline for 18 of 20 evaluators). IRT variants (1PL, 2PL, multidimensional) less consistent; compute time 1PL-IRT 1,782.75 vs EIP 0.00597.
limits: Difficulty is relative to the model pool.
agent_relevance: Cheap empirical difficulty from a panel of runs: a question that beats many attempts is hard. Counted, not judged.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Can 1B LLM Surpass 405B LLM? Rethinking Compute-Optimal Test-Time Scaling
finding: The best test-time method depends on problem difficulty, and difficulty is better defined by absolute pass rate than by quantile.
numbers: Qwen2.5-72B has Pass@1 above 80% on 76.2% of MATH-500, so quantile bins mislead. Absolute levels: easy 50-100%, medium 10-50%, hard 0-10% Pass@1. Policies under 7B: best-of-N for easy, beam search for hard; 7B-32B: DVTS for easy and medium, beam for hard; 72B: best-of-N at all levels.
limits: Math only, with process reward models. Optimal strategy shifts with model and reward model.
agent_relevance: Direct basis for an S0 gate: measure pass rate with a few cheap samples, then pick search depth by absolute thresholds, not rank.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 on digit-matrix problems shows human-like difficulty effects from rule number and relation type.
numbers: Digit matrices, 40 UCLA undergraduates. GPT-3 above average humans: generative OR 1.88 (CI 1.21-2.91), multiple choice OR 6.27. GPT-3 vs human pattern across problem types r(30)=0.39, p=0.027. Progression rules harder (human OR 0.41); more unique rules harder (human OR 0.61); spatially permuted logic problems harder (human OR 0.52).
limits: Modest pattern match (r 0.39).
agent_relevance: Embretson-style features (rule count, rule type, alignment) also drive model difficulty at least partly, so they can serve as S0 features for matrix-like tasks.

source: arXiv 2401.12117 (2024) The Curious Case of Nonverbal Abstract Reasoning with Multi-Modal Large Language Models
finding: Open multimodal LLMs score near chance on abstract matrix puzzles with zero-shot prompts, while humans find them easy.
numbers: Zero-shot accuracy within -8.7% to +7.3% of random on IQ50, -1.0% to +0.6% on RAVEN-S, -5.6% to +6.4% on CCSE. Human volunteers on 20% of IQ50: 95.9% accuracy (SD 6.92).
limits: 2024-era models.
agent_relevance: What is hard for people (rule count) does not predict what is hard for the model. Estimate difficulty with the solver in the loop.

source: ARC Prize Foundation (2025) ARC-AGI-2: A New Challenge for Frontier AI Reasoning Systems
finding: ARC-AGI-2 was built with an empirical difficulty index and human calibration across subsets.
numbers: 407 participants, 515 sessions, 1,848 unique task test pairs, 13,405 attempts, 62% solved; median 2.3 min per attempt. Task difficulty = share of participants fully correct. Public, semi-private and private sets matched to within 1 percentage point of mean human accuracy. No self-reported demographic factor predicted performance. A task advanced only if at least 2 participants solved a pair within 2 attempts.
limits: Paid volunteers ($5 per correct task, 90-minute sessions). Difficulty is for humans, not models.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that human pass rate is the item difficulty index behind the benchmark we are tested on.

source: ARC Prize Foundation (2025) ARC-AGI-2: A New Challenge for Frontier AI Reasoning Systems (ARC-AGI-1 problems)
finding: ARC-AGI-1 had no first-party human baseline and possibly uneven difficulty across subsets.
numbers: Two individuals scored 97% and 98% on the private set. 2020 competition top score 20%; later 49% of the private set was solved by at least one team. o3 preview 76% (low compute, about $200 per task) and 88% (high compute, about $20,000 per task).
limits: Subset inconsistency is the authors' stated concern; gaps not tabulated in the text read.
agent_relevance: Task difficulty varies between splits, so estimate it within the split you are tested on.

source: RIDE authors (2025) RIDE: Difficulty Evolving Perturbation with Item Response Theory for Mathematical Reasoning
finding: IRT-based difficulty is used as a reward for a rewriter that makes math questions harder, and models lose accuracy on the rewrites.
numbers: Mean performance drop rate 21.73% across 26 models on rewritten AIME-24 and AMC-23; largest case reached 88.90%.
limits: I did not check human validation of the rewritten difficulty.
agent_relevance: A closed loop where a difficulty estimate is the training signal. Not our setting, but shows IRT difficulty can steer item generation.

source: Search gap: no Embretson-style cognitive design system found inside an LLM agent loop
finding: No 2020-2026 paper found in the searches used Embretson's cognitive design system (stimulus features to difficulty, then item generation) inside an LLM agent loop.
numbers: Searches: arXiv API on item response theory + LLM benchmark; progressive matrices + language model; ARC + human task difficulty; test-time compute + difficulty. Web search quota ran out before a second sweep.
limits: Absence of evidence under a limited search.
agent_relevance: An S0 difficulty gate looks new as an agent-loop component. Nearest are pass-rate routing (Liu 2025) and hidden-state probes (Zhu 2025).

source: Cross-study pattern across the lines above: direct judged difficulty versus simulation or features
finding: Across 2025-26 studies, direct judged difficulty is weak, while simulated attempts, extracted features and pass-rate counts work.
numbers: Direct judgment: ENEM rho .31-.37; NAEP r -0.14 to 0.14; GPT-4 vs IRT Spearman .16-.61; data-science course rho 0.06. Simulation or features: NAEP r .75-.82; K-5 r up to .87 pooled; Hoyl r .78; SMART PCC up to .67.
limits: Synthesis of lines above. Settings differ (population averages, pooling, test sets).
agent_relevance: Design S0 as measured pass rate from a few cheap attempts plus named feature slots, never a self-rated label.
